name: Simplification and Approximation — BODMAS Speed and Smart Rounding
whatIsIt: Simplification is solving a mixed expression (brackets, 'of', division, multiplication, addition, subtraction all in one line) in the ONE correct order — BODMAS. Approximation is rounding each number in a big, messy expression to a nearby convenient value so you can estimate the answer in seconds instead of computing it exactly.
whyNeeded: Almost every quant section opens with 8-10 simplification/approximation questions worth quick, guaranteed marks — but only if the order of operations is automatic and rounding is done confidently. Getting the order wrong is the single most common reason for a 'silly mistake' on an otherwise easy question.
realLifeUses: Mentally checking a restaurant or shopping bill
Quant/reasoning sections of every competitive exam — always among the first questions
Estimating a total cost before an exact calculator check
Reading and simplifying formulas in science and finance

vocabulary.meaning: Brackets, Of, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction — the order to solve a mixed expression in.
A bar drawn over a group of terms (like a fraction bar) — solved first, even before brackets.
Rounding each number to a nearby convenient value to estimate the answer quickly.
Means multiply, but is solved right after brackets — before division and multiplication signs.

story.title: The Left-to-Right Trap
story.text: Kavya solves 8 + 4 × 2 by going left to right: '8 + 4 is 12, times 2 is 24!' Her tutor stops her: 'Multiplication comes before addition — always. Do the 4 × 2 first: that's 8. THEN add: 8 + 8 = 16.' Kavya is startled — same numbers, two totally different answers, just because of the order. 'BODMAS isn't a suggestion,' says her tutor, 'it's the one rule that makes sure everyone gets the same answer from the same expression.'
story.answerInStory: 16 — multiply first (4×2=8), then add (8+8=16), not left-to-right.

visual.caption: Same expression, 8 + 4 × 2 — going left-to-right gives 24, but the correct BODMAS order gives 16.

teachingGallery.title: BODMAS order, one step at a time
teachingGallery.note: Brackets → Of → Division → Multiplication → Addition → Subtraction. Do only ONE operation type per pass through the expression.

examples.caption: Multiply first: 2×3=6, then subtract: 18−6=12 — not (18−2) first.

standardMethod.summary: Scan the expression once per letter of BODMAS: solve every bracket, then every 'of', then every division (left to right), then every multiplication (left to right), then every addition/subtraction together left to right.
steps: Solve anything under a vinculum (bar) first, then innermost brackets outward.
Solve every 'of' (a multiply, but before ÷ and ×).
Solve every ÷ and × together, left to right, in the order they appear.
Solve every + and − together, left to right, in the order they appear.

alternateMethods.name: Approximation rounding
alternateMethods.whenToUse: When the question has 'approximately' or '≈' and exact decimals aren't needed.
steps: Round each number to the nearest convenient value (whole number, or nearest 10/100).
Compute with the rounded numbers — much faster mentally.
Pick the answer option closest to your estimate.
alternateMethods.example: 48.97 × 5.03 ≈ 49 × 5 = 245 (actual value is 246.36 — close enough to identify the right option).

alternateMethods.name: Bracket-first sweep
steps: Always clear the innermost, roundest bracket ( ) first.
Then curly { }, then square [ ] — working outward.
Re-check BODMAS inside each bracket as you clear it.
÷ and × together, left to right: 24 ÷ 4 = 6, then 6 × 2 = 12.
+ and − together, left to right: 12 + 6 = 18, then 18 − 3 = 15.

trickPractice.trick: One letter of BODMAS per pass
trickPractice.intro: Don't jump around — clear ALL of one operation type before moving to the next letter of BODMAS.

commonMistakes.mistake: Solving a mixed expression strictly left to right instead of following BODMAS (e.g. 8 + 4 × 2 as (8+4)×2).
commonMistakes.fix: Multiplication and division ALWAYS happen before addition and subtraction, no matter where they sit in the line. Scan for × and ÷ first.

commonMistakes.mistake: Solving division or multiplication before an 'of' that appears earlier in the expression.
commonMistakes.fix: 'Of' is solved right after brackets — before any ÷ or × sign — even though it also means 'multiply'.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding numbers so aggressively during approximation that the estimate lands closer to a wrong answer option.
commonMistakes.fix: Round to the nearest sensible unit (nearest 1, 10, or 100 depending on the numbers' size) — not to the nearest 1000 for numbers like 48.97.

easy.q: In BODMAS, which comes first: Division or Addition?
hintLadder: D comes before A in BODMAS.

hintLadder: O comes before D in BODMAS.

revisionCard.summary: BODMAS: Brackets, Of, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction — clear one letter completely (left to right) before moving to the next. 'Of' is a multiply but comes right after brackets. For approximation, round each number sensibly (nearest 1/10/100 depending on size) and compute the rounded expression for a fast, close estimate.

gameMission.title: The BODMAS Order Line
gameMission.brief: Line up the jungle's operation signs in the correct BODMAS order before the expression can be solved!

realLifeProject: Write down 3 real shopping-bill style expressions (like 'price of 3 items + 2 items on offer') and solve each with BODMAS, then check with a calculator.

rememberIt.hook: One letter of BODMAS at a time
rememberIt.unpack: Brackets, Of, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction — clear each fully before the next.

studentQuestions.q: Why does 'of' come before division if both are just multiplying?
studentQuestions.a: It's a fixed convention (Brackets, Of, Division, Multiplication...) so that everyone reading the same expression gets the same answer — without an agreed order, the same expression could mean different things to different people.

studentQuestions.q: How do I know how much to round during approximation?
studentQuestions.a: Round to a size that matches the numbers involved — nearest 1 for numbers under 10, nearest 10 for numbers in the hundreds, nearest 100 for numbers in the thousands. The goal is a close estimate, not perfect accuracy.
